newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Chastened British unions preach social harmony.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chastened British unions preach social harmony.

text.p: Britain's chastened trade unions, whose strike-happy image helped scupper the last Labour government in 1979, are now preaching social harmony and see themselves in a positive role if Labour wins a May election.

The unions may have helped found the Labour Party at the end of the last century but party leader Tony Blair is no sentimentalist and he has steadfastly refused to repeal the series of Conservative laws that neutered unions in the 1980s.
Swallowing hard, the leaders of the big trade unions have accepted this, happy enough with Labour's pledge to bring in a minimum wage and accept European Union workplace rules.
Some, like John Monks, general secretary of the union umbrella body, the Trades Union Congress (TUC), have gone further and actively embraced Blair's business-friendly agenda.

On March 20, Monks wrote to Britain's top 300 companies, offering them negotiations on how Europe's Social Chapter -- derided as anti-business by the present Conservative government -- could be introduced with the least disruption to industry.
"While the TUC does favour minimum workplace standards...we are not in favour of rigid rules that do not take account of the specifics of the British workplace," he wrote.
In February, the general council of the TUC, which includes leaders of all the big unions, adopted a document called "Partners for Progress", spelling out Monks' ideas.
Some analysts saw this as the union bosses doing a deal to help out Labour by sitting on pent-up frustrations on the shop floor, but Monks preferred a more positive interpretation.
"It's not a matter of "putting a lid on strikes', but a genuine effort to minimise disputes, to avoid strikes, using arbitration, mediation and conciliation," he told reporters.
The emphasis on workplace issues and the avoidance of confrontation was emphasised by John Edmonds, general secretary of the big GMB general union.
"People nowadays don't like strikes -- I don't think they ever did," he said in an interview."If there is a strike now you can be absolutely sure there is just cause."
PENDULUM SWUNG TO EMPLOYERS AFTER TROUBLED 1970'S
Provisional estimates show that 1.30 million days were lost to strikes in 1996.
That is well up on the 410,000 lost in 1995 and 280,000 in 1994 -- the lowest since records began -- but it is a far cry from the average 6.7 million days lost in the 20 years to 1994.

But even the new, business-friendly Labour Party thinks the pendulum has swung too far in the bosses' favour and, although it will not be repealing the Conservatives' union laws, it will be making it easier for unions to organise in the workplace.
For example, if a majority of workers in a company vote for union representation, an employer will be obliged to negotiate with it on pay, hours, holidays and training.
There may also be a right to strike for the first time. Currently, workers can be dismissed even if a strike is legal.
"The rights of employees in Britain have been reduced very substantially," Edmonds said.
"Frankly, when you make comparisons, you get to countries like the Philippines having better levels of protection, particularly for part-time workers, than we have."
Labour's pledge to bring in a minimum wage and sign up to the Social Chapter should not trouble industry, Monks said.

"The balance of employers are prepared to sign up to a Social Europe and will accept a minimum wage. Their ambition is to stop too much coming out of a Social Chapter and a minimum wage that is too high. We're moving beyond the arguments of principle to one of practicality," he said in an interview.
The unions have been cowed by the Conservatives' anti-union laws which, along with the demise of heavy industry, have helped cut membership in half since the 1970s to about seven million.

Some political analysts have predicted renewed militancy and a push for higher wages if Labour wins power, especially in the public services, where a government pay freeze and the introduction of private sector operators have combined to cut take-home pay.
Monks felt this would be manageable. "I don't think people are unrealistic. I don't think you vote Labour for a bloody great pay increase. It doesn't happen like that," he said.
But he added: "I don't think (government) can indefinitely lean on public sector workers."
MINIMUM WAGE HIGH ON UNIONS' AGENDA
The leaders of Britain's biggest unions have generally kept their feelings to themselves in the run-up to the election.
Even Rodney Bickerstaffe, the leader of 1.4 million public sector workers grouped in Unison, has been restrained.

"We know that employment will be Labour's first priority, but we also want to see fairness, particularly for the people at the bottom of the pay rung, which includes thousands of low-paid public sector workers," he said.

Fairness for him means the speedy introduction of a minimum wage. Monks reckoned it might take up to 12 months before a minimum wage was introduced, given the time needed for the planned Low Pay Commission to report and to push a bill through parliament, but the unions could live with that, he said.
"If people see Labour is determined to carry that out and there has to be debating time in parliament for it...that's just how long things take," he said.

However, Labour leaders are thought to favour a minimum wage some way below the 4.26 pounds ($7) an hour backed by the TUC's annual conference, against Monks's wishes, in September, and the issue could provide an early test of Labour-union relations.

In the old days, union leaders like Bickerstaffe, Edmonds and Monks had a direct line to Labour ministers. Monks does not expect that this time round, but he expects union arguments to be given a hearing, something that has not happened since 1979.
"It would be very nice to operate in an atmosphere where hostility is not one of the key things, where there is a keen awareness to work together," he said.
"It's time for a change rather than time for hostility." ($1=.6124 Pound)
